description:
Start with a real project

Pick a paragraph that you wrote or can revise. Mark the facts, terms and quotations that must survive the edit.

Review the first version

Compare each revised sentence with the source. Restoring a missing qualification matters more than making the writing sound smoother.

Check the final result

Keep citations attached to their claims and confirm your school or client's rules before submitting assisted writing.

Frequently asked questions

Does paraphrasing remove the need to cite?

Keep the citation when the underlying idea or evidence came from another source.

Start with a passage that has one clear problem

Smodin can help with rewriting and other writing tasks. Pick a passage that you wrote or have permission to edit. Read it once and say what makes it hard to follow. A paragraph may use too many long sentences. It may bury the main point near the end. It may use different words for the same product. A specific problem gives you a useful way to judge the rewrite.

Keep the original in a separate column or document. Mark details that must stay the same, including dates, figures, quoted words, and any condition attached to a claim. If the source says a service usually takes three working days after approval, the revision needs both the time estimate and the approval condition. Changing either detail could give the reader the wrong expectation.

Compare the rewrite sentence by sentence

Ask for one change at a time. Start with shorter sentences or simpler language. Put the result beside the source and check whether each new sentence carries the same meaning. Look for words that make a cautious claim sound certain. If “can help” becomes “will solve,” decide whether the evidence supports that stronger wording.

A good revision can also change the order. Suppose a help article opens with three paragraphs about account settings before it tells the customer where to click. Move the action to the first paragraph. Keep the background next to the step it explains. Read the new version aloud to check whether the instructions sound like something you would say to a real customer.

Use a summary to review the structure

Summarize the section in one sentence after you revise it. Then read the surrounding headings. If two sections have the same summary, combine them or give each a distinct question to answer. This can reveal repetition before it becomes a problem across the whole article.

When you summarize someone else's work, keep the reference with the idea. Check names, numbers, and dates against the original. A shorter version can leave out details that do not matter to your reader, but it should preserve the limits of the claim. If the source only studied one group or time period, keep that context where it affects how the reader should interpret the result.

Run a practical test before choosing access

Take a public paragraph from your own site and make two edits. In the first, shorten the sentences. In the second, explain a technical word for a beginner. Check which version is easier to read and whether you had to restore any facts. Record the time you spent on writing and review so you can compare the full process with your normal workflow.

Confirm which Smodin tools and usage limits apply to the SEOGBTools offer. If your work depends on a language, document length, or a particular editing feature, ask about that item directly. Keep copies of the original and approved drafts where you can review them again. For a different workflow focused on client emails and copy editing, see the HyperWrite product guide.

Make a revision brief before opening the tool

Write one line about the reader. A paragraph for a new customer can use familiar words and explain the first step. A paragraph for a team that already knows the service can move directly to the decision they need to make. Knowing who will read the piece helps you decide what to explain and what they already understand.

Add one line about the job of the text. A return policy should tell someone whether they can send an item back and how to start. An article introduction should help a visitor see whether the page answers their question. An internal note might tell a teammate who owns a task and when it needs to be done. Use that job to review the rewrite.

Finally, list the facts and terms that need to stay. Keep the list short enough to use while you edit. For a policy, it might include the date the period starts, the length of the period, and one exception. For a product page, it might include the product name, size, and what comes in the box. Set aside details you still need to verify.

Work through a customer help example

Imagine a shop wants to revise this sentence: “Returns may be initiated within fourteen days of delivery for unused items, subject to the exclusion of products made to order.” The information is there, but it takes time to read. Before rewriting, the editor marks the period, when it starts, the condition of the item, and the exception.

A clearer version can use two sentences. “You can start a return within 14 days after delivery if the item is unused. Made-to-order products are excluded.” The change keeps the meaning and makes the exception easier to see. The editor can then add a separate sentence explaining where to start a return if the shop has an approved process for that.

Compare the version with the full policy. If the shop starts the return period when an order is collected, the example may only apply to deliveries. If some made-to-order goods have a separate process, add that detail from the actual policy. A revision is ready when it matches the rule readers will face, including the conditions that apply to their case.

Keep technical terms where readers need them

Some difficult words belong in a guide because a reader will see them on screen or in a document. Keep the exact label and explain it once. For example, a software guide can tell someone to select “Export” and then say that this saves a copy of their work. If you replace the button label with a different word, the instructions become harder to follow.

Watch for terms with meanings that depend on the subject. In a store, a variant may mean one size or color of a product. In a writing guide, it may mean a second version of a passage. Define the term in the way your reader will use it. Keep the wording consistent after the first explanation.

When an unfamiliar word appears several times, decide which uses need the formal term. A heading can use the word a reader will search for, while the paragraph underneath gives a short explanation. A list of steps can repeat the exact label where someone needs to recognize it. Use the simple explanation where a person needs to make sense of what happens next.

Check summaries against the source

Choose a passage with one main finding and a few supporting details. Before using a summarizer, write your own one-sentence description of the finding. Then compare that sentence, the summary, and the original text. If they emphasize different points, read the source again and ask which point the evidence actually supports.

For example, a project report may say that five people found a new search box more quickly during a short test. A summary that says all customers will find products faster adds a claim the report did not make. A better summary can say that five test participants found the search box sooner and give the test conditions if they matter to the reader.

Use different lengths for different purposes. A one-sentence summary may help an editor decide where a section belongs. A two-paragraph summary may help a teammate understand the findings and limitations. If you need the full reasoning for a decision, keep a link to the original report and point to the section that explains it.

Preserve quotations and citations

Mark direct quotations before revising. Keep the wording as it appears in the source when you plan to quote it. If you explain the idea in your own words, keep the source attached. A reader needs a way to find the evidence even when the wording is new.

Check what each reference supports. A source that explains a general method may give you background without supporting a specific claim about a tool. A vendor help page may document a feature without saying it is available through a separate offer. If two claims rely on different sources, make it clear which source supports each claim.

Give sources descriptive titles in your notes. “Delivery policy, updated 3 May” is easier to check than a long URL on its own. Save the date where the terms might change. Before you publish, open each link and check whether a reader can reach the page you cited.

Review tone across a full article

Read all the headings together before editing each paragraph. A good order lets the reader see where they are in the explanation. In a guide to rewriting, the headings could move from preparing the source, to comparing the first revision, to checking quotes and references. A heading about choosing an access plan belongs where readers are ready to make that choice.

Then read the transitions between sections. If a section introduces a new term, explain why the reader needs it at that point. If two sections repeat the same advice, move the strongest example to the section where it helps most. Removing a repeated paragraph often makes the remaining explanation easier to use.

Finally, check the first and last lines. The opening should help readers recognize the problem. The last section can give them a short way to put the advice to work. A passage that begins with “Select a public paragraph and mark three facts you need to keep” gives readers a practical first action.

Create a review routine for a writing team

Agree on who owns the facts and who owns the final edit. A product manager may be able to verify a feature or a condition. An editor can check the order, tone, and consistency across the page. If one person does both jobs, use two passes. Start with accuracy, then read again for clarity.

Keep a copy of the original and the revised version. Add a note when an edit changes a key promise or removes a point. This makes it easier to explain the revision to a reviewer. It also gives the team a way to restore an important detail if it was dropped during a later pass.

Use a small checklist at handoff. Include the source, the intended reader, and any outstanding question. If a passage still needs a price or a policy date, make that visible in the working file. Before you move the text into a public page, confirm that every open item has been handled.

Decide whether the tool fits the work you do

Try two pieces of writing with different needs. Use one short help paragraph to test simple language. Use a longer section to see how well you can keep the main point and source references together. Compare the time spent preparing, editing, and checking each result. Note any feature you need every week.

Check access to the specific Smodin tools you want to use. Ask which limits apply to the document size and language you plan to work with. If you have client material, check your client's rules for entering it into an outside service. A public help article or an example with invented details is enough for a first test.

More questions about Smodin

Can I revise a whole page in one pass?

You can review the page as a whole for order and repetition. For detailed changes, working section by section makes it easier to catch missing facts. Read the full page again afterward to check that the terms and tone match across sections.

How do I know if a rewrite changed the meaning?

Look at what each version promises, who it applies to, and when it applies. A sentence can sound close to the original while changing one of those points. If you are unsure, ask someone to read both versions and tell you what they would expect to happen.

What is a good use for a short summary?

A short summary can help you decide whether a section belongs in a longer article. It can also give a teammate a quick view of a source before they read the details. Keep any conditions that affect the meaning and include the source when the summary relies on someone else's work.

Can I use a rewriting tool for school work?

Check your institution's rules for the assignment and follow any requirements for disclosure. Keep track of the sources you used and preserve quotations as written. Ask the instructor if the rules leave the kind of editing you want to do unclear.
